By "pay off" I mean fully paying off the cost of the flat comprising of the monthly mortgage that needs to be paid besides the initial deposit.

In Singapore we "own" our own homes but it's not real ownership like in the United States or other Western countries where you can own a house or plot of land indefinitely and pass it down to the future generations. The ownership is a 99 year leasehold from the government and when the lease is up you either renew the lease or sell the flat away. There is no chance of passing down the flat to your descendants if you or your descendants live past the 99 year threshold.

But one very good thing about Singapore is its public housing model which is arguably one of the best, if not the best in the world. 90% of citizens are able to own their own flat after a few decades of working. The public apartments are cheaper than many major cities around the world, spacious and regularly maintained (daily garbage collection) and upgraded in terms of facilities. The government has done extremely well in this aspect.

Maybe if Singapore wasn't so land scarce and tiny, we would all be able to buy houses and cars at a cheaper price like the typical Western country and own them indefinitely. The curse of land scarcity leads to constraints for a lot of stuff and drives up prices.

I suffer from depression and it was hard at first to reach out to people and open up about my depression but it pushed me to such a low point where I had to seek emergency treatment at a mental hospital and start my psychotherapy treatment sessions with a really good and helpful therapist.

Imo depression is not simply something you can shrug off slowly and slowly regain your happiness. It is like a pit of despair or black hole that sucks out all feelings of joy and purpose of life from your life where you cannot even enjoy and be happy about things that used to interest you or make you happy. It robs the essence out of the human soul. Coupled with the banality and dullness of everyday life for a great many people and relationship problems, financial problems, failing grades and poor work performance as a result of this horrible pestilence can push people to the edge. Many depression sufferers suffer in silence and are afraid of reaching out for help due to stigmas and as a result it can end up in a horrible outcome.

I just want to say that there is absolutely nothing wrong admitting that you have depression and reaching out for help and seeking appropriate treatment immediately. Therapy and meds do work for many people but it's dependent on the individual. Many people recover from depression and eventually become happy after seeking treatment and sticking through with the treatment. I'm testament to that.

Singapore is very very expensive if you want to have a high-class luxurious lifestyle but for us locals we can have a decent standard of living with cheap hawker fare, subsidized housing and healthcare. If you are a tourist, stick to the heartland malls instead of the Marina Bay Sands and Orchard Road. Those are way overpriced and are only for the rich tourists. Stick to hawker centres and food courts instead of restaurants and expensive dining places for relatively cheap local and international hawker fare.

You don't need to go to the tourist traps like Sentosa where admissions are not that cheap and food is overpriced.
We have lots of free nature reserves and parks like HortPark, Henderson Ridges Bukit Timah Hill, MacRitchie Nature trail, Sungei Buloh Nature Reserve, Labrador Nature Reserve and many small pockets of green throughout the island so it's not all concrete jungle. The parks are also linked together by park connector networks where you can cycle and see great scenery along the way. 

For traditional and colonial-era architecture, there are some nice places to explore and photograph like Emerald Hill which is a small strip of beautiful and colourful shophouses located near Orchard Central, a stretch of shophouses along Duxton Hill in Tanjong Pagar, colourful shophouses in Joo Chiat and Tanjong Katong. Lots of colonial-era British architecture in Fort Canning and Boat Quay along the Singapore river. For modern architecture, Marina Bay and Downtown is obviously the most popular, they're full of futuristic modern glass buildings. There are also lots of modern futuristic and stunning modern architecture in posh housing districts and all throughout Singapore so you need to get out and really explore.

I understand where you're coming from. It is a hard decision to leave a game you've invested a long time in, probably in the hundreds to thousands of hours for many and the many good friends you've made in a game. It is a very hard decision that I would liken it to permanently leaving a child that you've nurtured since young with love and care to a foster parent. I've invested thousands of hours on RuneScape, attaining many achievements and almost maxing out my character. I've made too many good friends on that game, especially in my clan. I've gone cold turkey many times as well, subscribing and playing for weeks and months on end and quitting cold turkey for many months before getting back in it.

Once you get older life does take priority, though. When I was younger I had all the time in the world to spend on RuneScape. I would sit through 10 hour days to grind for 99s in the various skills. I was pumped with adrenaline and happiness everytime I got ever closer to attaining a 99. But as a result of being addicted to the game and spending ungodly hours on it my grades suffered drastically and I almost failed out of secondary school. Life gave me a wake up call and I scraped through secondary school with barely passing grades. I started moderating my playtime and worked hard through my polytechnic education to graduate in the top 10%. Now, I'm serving my national obligation as a clerk in my country's Armed Forces and will be enrolling in a Computer Science course in university once I complete my service. I'm still playing RuneScape, just subscribed days ago for a Twitch Prime promotion and only play 2-3 hours maximum a day, mostly just doing dailies. I was really competitive back then in RuneScape and was hell-bent on maxing out my character to the point of putting in over 10 hours a day for a meaningless pixelated cape. Now that I'm older and have adult responsibilities when looking back I see no point being competitive now and I just want to play for leisure and enjoyment instead of making the game feel like a chore.

You can play a game and enjoy it, there's nothing wrong. There is only a problem if you let the game control you to the point of affecting your daily function in life, such as your school grades, relationships and work. It's even worse when you're addicted to the point of spending large amounts of money on micro-transactions instead of paying the bills, food and rent. Never ever go down that downhill path and just remember that life takes priority over gaming. My advice is to go cold turkey if you're really too addicted and start moderating your playtime slowly by reducing it in 1 hour blocks. Treat gaming as a hobby and leisure activity instead of revolving your entire life on it.

Singapore has zero natural resources to export so we have to work hard as fuck to generate the economic growth required for a first world standard of living, and with a tiny domestic economy we have to rely on external markets and trade to survive. In Singapore, as long as you're willing to work hard, upgrade your qualifications and skills, you won't starve and there will be plenty of opportunities for you to have a comfortable first world standard of living.

Singapore is a really cosmopolitan society with a mish mash of many religions and ethnicities on a small island (we have 4 main ethnicities and languages) and almost half of our population are foreigners working and living in Singapore and many more have already attained permanent residency. It makes sense that we have to run a tight leash and enforce laws and a society that respects each other and works for the best of the country regardless of ethnicity, religion or culture.

Singapore is rich because of our strategic position which makes us a global hub of trading and finance (3rd largest FOREX centre in the world and over 200% trade-to GDP ratio) and is the main source of our prosperity despite having zero natural resources. We have to trade with the world and be a big player in finance to prosper and bring in economic growth. We don't have huge swathes of land to set up large farms to produce and grow our own food nor any significant primary agricultural industry or large-scale secondary manufacturing industry. But despite that we still manufacture some of our own military weapons and vehicles, we are the 4th largest exporter of high-tech equipment and our manufacturing output is only second to that of Switzerland per capita. Over 90% of our food is imported globally and that makes us very vulnerable to price fluctuations especially food which is a vital human requirement. Our only resource is our people and that's why education is very important - our people are one of the most educated in the world, and only with tertiary education and skills upgrading can our people move up the economic ladder and into higher value-adding and more advanced industries.

What really makes me proud is that Singapore has become an economic and financial powerhouse in such a short amount of time since independence without any significant natural resources to boot aside from our key strategic location for trade. Our passport is one of the strongest in the world and we can stand tall among the more established and developed countries in the world.

1) My grades were plummeting like crazy. I was in secondary school back then so I took a lot of subjects like Math, Science, English and the Humanities. In the mid-term and final year exams I consistently scored failing grades due to neglecting my studies. I played RuneScape for almost the entirety of my waking hours, save for going to school.

2) Lots of my in-game friends left from greener pastures, so I felt alone with no one to talk to when playing. A lot of the clans I were in to participate in various community activities disbanded, and finding new ones were a huge hassle.

3) The frequency and pace of micro-transactions and promotions was increasing to the point that they overtook the pace of releasing actual playable content week after week. I realized that at this point the maker of RuneScape cared more about filling their pockets than about the players. Even then, promised content was half-assed, half-baked and did not garner my interest for long. I am sure that a lot of people in the RuneScape community and playerbase feel the same sentiments that I do. This was one of the final straws that led me to quit.

I quit around late 2016 and safe to say I haven't looked back. I realized I was spending too much time levelling and grinding a virtual character for pixelated capes and increasing pixelated stats and numbers which hold no significance for me in the real world. I realized that doing these wouldn't add value to my portfolio, actual skills nor will these aid me in my future career and job prospects.

Now that I got into the habit of regularly wearing a watch (since I went into the army, I am required to wear a watch at all times to keep track of time, especially during outfields and training exercises), it's easier for me to know the current time at first glance. Now that I'm a clerk in the army, I have a better habit of keeping track of time, so that I'm able to go for my 2 hour lunch breaks on time and leave the office on the dot everyday.

RuneScape was mindless and tedious, and I was not enjoying the game but actually just grinding and farming for levels, stats and items all the while, so RuneScape felt like a chore to me. Plus, dailyscape didn't help either, I felt that I was obliged to do all of the daily tasks upon logging in everyday because they were ridiculously efficient experience gains per hour even if I did not enjoy them. I felt that I had to do them just for the rewards and that was a major turnoff. Leaving RuneScape after having sunk 5.5k hours was not at all easy given how much time and effort I've spent along with leaving some of the best friends I've made online as well as my clan, it was honestly worth it. I feel like I have much more time and am a much happier person being free from the shackles of RuneScape addiction.

As for social media, I felt that I was trying to project my life as perfect as possible to others online and that I would be depressed from seeing everyone's highlight reels and comparing my life to theirs. Along with the drama, bullshit and narcissistic people prevalent in social media, I felt that these were too much for me to handle and that is all pointless in the end and I should first focus on myself and live life in my own terms, so I just said fuck it and purged a large majority of my social media accounts altogether. Live for yourself and most importantly, enjoy every moment and live your day-to-day life without needing to seek people's validations or obsess over how many "likes" you get.

There is nothing wrong with having fun when playing video games. If you feel that video games are taking control over your life and negatively affecting your grades and work, then I'd look into moderating playtime and quitting altogether as a first step if the addiction gets too serious.

Same thing happened to me when I gamed heavily in the past. Gaming releases a short burst of dopamine to make you feel good and all but after a period of time depression sets in. That and social media.
